title: The Effect of Teacher Feedback on the Simple Past Tense Acquisition in Senior High School Students' English Writing
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher written corrective feedback improves senior high school students’ English writing, specifically their acquisition of the simple past tense in narrative compositions. The study addresses a long-running debate in second-language writing research over whether direct feedback, where teachers supply the correct form, or indirect feedback, where teachers indicate errors without correcting them, is more effective. It also asks how students perceive these two forms of teacher feedback.

The intervention compared two teacher-feedback approaches in regular school writing instruction. One class received direct feedback, with the teacher correcting students’ simple past tense errors; the other received indirect feedback, with the teacher underlining or pointing out errors but not providing the correction. Students completed a pretest, four writing tasks, a posttest, and a questionnaire. The quantitative component analyzed grammar test and writing-task scores, while the questionnaire captured students’ attitudes and preferences toward feedback.

Participants were 63 senior high school students from two classes in a single Chinese high school, taught by the same teacher. The writing tasks were narrative writing assignments focused on use of the simple past tense. The intervention lasted about two months. The school context was a classroom-based English as a foreign language setting, and the target outcome was grammatical accuracy in writing rather than broader holistic writing quality.

The study concludes that both direct and indirect teacher feedback were associated with improvement from pretest to posttest in students’ simple past tense accuracy. However, there was no statistically significant difference between the direct- and indirect-feedback groups on the writing-task comparisons, so neither feedback type clearly outperformed the other. Questionnaire results indicated that students valued teacher feedback and generally preferred direct feedback, especially correction of grammar errors. Overall, the paper supports teacher feedback as beneficial in this high school EFL writing context, while suggesting that the choice between direct and indirect feedback may depend on students’ needs rather than one method being universally superior.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small two-group comparative classroom study with pre/post testing and questionnaire data, but it does not report random assignment, effect sizes, or strong controls against selection and implementation bias. The methodology is clearer than an opinion piece, yet it falls short of a well-designed experimental or quasi-experimental study.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant within-group improvement under both teacher feedback conditions, but no clear advantage of one comparator over the other and no standardized effect sizes. Impact on high school writing quality is therefore positive but uncertain in magnitude and limited to a narrow grammar-focused outcome.

finding.finding_summary: In a two-class high school EFL writing study, both teacher direct feedback and teacher indirect feedback were associated with significant pretest-to-posttest gains in students' accuracy on the English simple past tense, a writing-relevant language feature. Among the 63 students who completed all four writing tasks, the direct-feedback group improved from Mean=8.03 (SD=3.886) to Mean=14.10 (SD=3.155) on a 20-item sentence-correction test, and the indirect-feedback group improved from Mean=9.13 (SD=3.635) to Mean=13.28 (SD=3.485); however, between-group comparisons on writing tasks showed no significant difference between direct and indirect feedback conditions (reported Sig. values .369, .145, .636).
finding.measure: Accuracy of simple past tense in English writing and sentence-correction tests; writing task scores across four narrative writing assignments
finding.std_deviation: Direct pre/post SD=3.886/3.155; Indirect pre/post SD=3.635/3.485

finding.finding_summary: Questionnaire results indicated that students in both classes valued teacher feedback and believed it helped improve their writing. Most students reported a preference for direct teacher feedback over indirect feedback, even though the study found no significant performance difference between the two feedback types on the main writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire on attitudes, preferences, and expectations regarding teacher feedback
